                                              PROJECT NO. 58481

 RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT                               §      PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION                            §
 STANDARDS UNDER PURA § 37.0561                        §                    OF TEXAS


     OFFICE OF PUBLIC UTILITY COUNSEL’S COMMENTS REGARDING THE
            PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION OF NEW 16 TAC §25.194

       The Office of Public Utility Counsel (OPUC), representing the interests of residential

and small commercial consumers in Texas, respectfully submits these comments in response to

the Public Utility Commission of Texas’s (PUCT or Commission) proposal for publication (PFP)

to implement large load interconnection standards under Public Utility Regulatory Act

(PURA) § 37.0561 enacted by Senate Bill 6, 89th Texas Legislature, Regular Session (SB 6). 1

OPUC recognizes the Commission’s resolute effort to balance protecting residential and small

commercial consumers while keeping Texas open for business and maintaining a reliable grid in

the rulemaking process. OPUC appreciates the PUCT’s continued endeavor to evaluate competing

stakeholder interests as it develops the final rule language for large load interconnection standards.

The PFP establishes an April 17, 2026 deadline for stakeholders to file initial comments. 2 Thus,

these comments are timely filed.

                                         I.      SB 6 LANGUAGE

                                   II.     APPLICABILITY

       Under the current PFP language, proposed 16 Tex. Admin. Code (TAC) § 25.194 would

not apply to existing large load customers that are over 76 MW and apply for interconnection that

is less than 75 MW. This gap allows these large load customers to incrementally increase their

load by 74 MW without ever undergoing the large load interconnection criteria. Although the

expanded load is less than 75 MW, the customer is still over 75 MW, and thus a “large load

customer.” Pursuant to PURA § 37.0561, the large load interconnection standards must apply to

“a new or expanded interconnection where the total load at a single site would exceed a demand

threshold established by the commission based on the size of loads that significantly impact

transmission needs in the ERCOT power region.” 13 To the extent that transmission is built to serve

these customers’ expanded load, and such customers later decide not to expand operations—those

transmission costs are still considered stranded and should not be passed on to other ratepayers.

As such, the PFP language should be revised to apply to these types of large load customers.

       Alternatively, if the Commission finds that these types of customers do not “significantly

impact transmission needs”, then OPUC recommends including some type of evaluation on

transmission needs at each request. For example, no significant transmission impact may occur

with the first expansion request for 74 MW, but the second expansion request may require a new

substation to be built or new lines put in because the existing system cannot take on new energy

                                    III.    SITE CONTROL

       A. Make the progress reports mandatory rather than “upon request.”

       OPUC generally supports the PFP language regarding site-related studies, engineering

services, and state and local regulatory approvals. OPUC would encourage the Commission to

strengthen this site control language by removing the “upon request” language and impose a

requirement that the large load provide the quarterly updates or progress reports. If an end user is

serious about materializing and conducting operations at the requested point of interconnection,

they will show efforts made to procure the necessary equipment, contracts, regulatory approvals,

permitting, etc. to develop and conduct business at that physical location.

       B. Require large load customers that are developers to show proof of contracts or serious
          negotiations with large load customers that will operate at the facility for which
          transmission is built to serve.

       If the “large load customer” requesting interconnection is a developer rather than the actual

end use company (i.e. data center, chemical plant, AI, etc.), then OPUC recommends adding a

provision to the site control requirement that the developer must produce to the interconnecting

utility and ERCOT proof of contracts with actual large load customer(s) or provide demonstration

of good faith efforts to procure contracts with large load customers to operate at the site. If the

developer is in conversations with the large load customers about operating at that facility or in

initial talks with such customers, but those customers subsequently choose to operate elsewhere—




                                                 5
 the project could lead to stranded transmission costs that other ratepayers have to pay. 14 Requiring

the developer to demonstrate evidence of serious intent by the large load customer to operate at

the facility will help preclude this situation from occurring.

         It has been asserted that if a large load customer does not show up, several more are in line

to take its place. OPUC recognizes ERCOT’s interconnection queue currently has a long waitlist.

However, agency rules are not designed for trends, but for the unknown. What may be true today

could all change tomorrow or five years from now based on unforeseen circumstances. There is

no guarantee that other large load customers will take the place of another large customer that

backs out.

         For example, CenterPoint Energy Houston Electric, LLC (CenterPoint) received approval

from the ERCOT board of directors in September 2025 for a transmission project costing

approximately $545 million in the Baytown area to interconnect a particular large load customer. 15

After approval was granted but before construction started, the load customer subsequently

announced that it was indefinitely pausing the planned project in Baytown. To date, no other large

load customer has requested to interconnect at that location. CenterPoint has since re-evaluated

the transmission needed to maintain a reliable grid without the large load interconnection and

submitted its modification request to ERCOT. 16

         C. Require the large load customer to disclose to the interconnecting utility provider and
           ERCOT the customer’s expected water usage and water supply source(s).

        It is OPUC’s understanding that several types of large load customers require significant

water usage to conduct business. Given the statewide concern about Texas’s water supply, and

several local areas in water supply crisis, 17 knowing whether the large load customer has sufficient

water supply to operate is a significant element in evaluating whether the customer will materialize

and conduct business at the requested site in the foreseeable future.

        The rule should require large load customers to disclose detailed information as to their

anticipated water usage, the source of that water supply, and whether such supply is sourced within

Texas. For loads relying on Texas-based water supplies, the rule should further require

identification and disclosure of contingency plans or alternative water sources in the event drought

conditions or other constraints limit availability.

        Requiring this level of transparency will help ensure that interconnection decisions

account for resource adequacy beyond electric infrastructure and reduce the risk of stranded costs

or operational disruptions associated with insufficient water supply. As an example, a

major industrial and data center project in Indiana is expected to require up to

eight million gallons per day (MGD) of water in a city that averages about two MGD, with peak

demand just over three MGD. 18 To accommodate this increase, a $560 million water supply project

                                              IV.     STUDY FEE

        The PFP is unclear as to whether a large load that requests additional capacity after

completion of the screening study is required to pay a new study fee associated with the increased

capacity request. To be consistent with SB 6 requirements, 21 rule language should be added to

clarify that any large load requesting additional capacity after the interconnection study in

proposed subparagraph (e) is completed must pay an additional study fee. OPUC recognizes that

the actualities associated with the batch study process’s adoption may impact the rule language

needed to address large load customers requesting additional capacity after the initial transmission

screening is conducted, and encourages the Commission to adopt language that will encompass

the batch study process.


                                 V.      FINANCIAL COMMITMENTS

        A. General Concerns

        OPUC’s principal concern is ensuring that all costs accrued to interconnect a large load to

the ERCOT grid are paid for by the large load customer and not passed on to residential and small

commercial consumers. As long as this end is achieved, OPUC is generally impartial to the means

for accomplishing that objective. With that said, OPUC is cognizant that without (1) clear

definitions of direct interconnection costs, CIAC, and system upgrades, (2) processes for the

determination of each, and (3) language for how the provisions in this project and the transmission

cost allocation in Project No. 58484 22 intertwine, there will be costs accrued by large load

customers that fall through the cracks and end up being passed on to other ratepayers.

         Even now, there are several transmission projects estimated to cost billions of dollars that

have been approved by ERCOT within the last year, or up for approval at the next board meeting,

where the costs will likely be distributed under the existing four coincident peak (4CP) method.

Based on the data presented in Commission Staff’s (Staff) Draft Evaluation, average individual

Texans will bear 40% or more of those costs. 23

        Because there has not yet been a decision or direction from the Commission in

Project No. 58484 24 as to how transmission costs should be allocated, OPUC’s comments on the

PFP’s financial security provisions will be overly comprehensive to ensure there is no gap in large

load customers contributing to the recovery of interconnection costs that would not have accrued

but for the large loads’ interconnection requests.

        B. Annually evaluate the financial security based on a dollar per megawatt basis.

        The PFP states that “[b]eginning in 2027, the commission will adjust the $50,000 value on

January 1 every five years.” 25 Given the importance of this standard as part of the “uniform

financial commitment requirements for the development of transmission infrastructure needed to

serve a large load customer,” 26 OPUC recommends that the commission evaluate and adjust the

value every year. This ensures that the financial security per MW stays consistent with

contemporary equipment and labor costs that are necessary to build the transmission infrastructure

to connect the large load customer.

         C. Increase the financial security based on a dollar per megawatt basis, or alternatively,
           implement a phased amount based on the load customer size.

               1. Increase the financial security to $100,000 per megawatt.

        Section 35.004(c-1) requires large load customers to contribute to costs accrued to

interconnect and energize that customer to the grid. 27 Section 37.0561(h) provides that the large

load interconnection standards established by the Commission “must include uniform financial

commitment requirements for the development of transmission infrastructure needed to serve a

large load customer subject to Subsection (c).” The statute continues that “[t]he standards must

provide that satisfactory proof of financial commitment may include” and enumerates several

options. 28

        OPUC interprets PURA § 37.0561(h) as requiring large load customers to show financial

proof that they are financially capable of paying for “the interconnecting electric utility’s costs to

interconnect the large load to the utility’s system;” 29 whereas PURA §§ 35.004(c-1) and

37.0561(h), read together, require that a large load customer have the financial capability to pay

for all costs accrued to interconnect the large load customer. If a large load customer does not

have the financial capability to pay for the construction and operation of a facility now, then that

could result in the large customer not materializing or backing out of the interconnection request

for lack of funding.

        Additionally, there are concerns regarding how the proposed framework operates in the

context of ERCOT’s batch study process. Based on OPUC’s understanding, under ERCOT’s

planned based on the aggregate demand of that group, there is no mechanism to address cost

recovery if a portion of those large loads withdraw from the process. In such circumstances,

ERCOT does not reallocate the unused capacity to new customers within the same batch, nor does

it require the remaining projects to increase their financial contributions to reflect the reduced

participation. Consequently, the costs of transmission infrastructure built to serve withdrawn

projects may ultimately be shifted to residential and small commercial consumers through future

rate proceedings.

       OPUC understands that stakeholders have suggested this concern is mitigated in situations

where a large load withdraws prior to the execution of an interconnection agreement where no

transmission has yet been constructed. While this may be true for early-stage withdrawals, there

remains a possibility that large loads withdraw after the refinement period study or once

construction has started. At that stage, transmission planning decisions are more likely to have

advanced and construction activities could have started or be imminent. Cognizant that financial

security posted for network upgrades in the interconnection agreement may provide for relief,

OPUC contends the existing framework may not adequately ensure that the costs associated with

serving the withdrawn load are reassigned to cost-causing projects. Instead, those costs may be

shifted to all rate payers, contrary to the principle of cost causation. This gap underscores the need

for a higher financial security requirement to protect residential and small commercial consumers

from bearing large load interconnection and transmission costs.

       Moreover, several of the transmission projects currently approved by or in the process of

approval with ERCOT are in the millions or billions of dollars. The dollar per MW amount does

 not cover the cost of those approved transmission projects requested to interconnect particular

large load customers.

        This issue is emerging across the ERCOT region with multiple transmission service

providers. Several recent Regional Planning Group (RPG) projects involve billions of dollars in

transmission infrastructure driven primarily by large load interconnections. For example, the

South Texas Electric Cooperative’s Nueces Green Ammonia project, scheduled for consideration

at ERCOT’s April Board of Directors meeting, carries an estimated cost of $161 million and is

designed primarily to serve a 1,150 MW load. 30 Applying the $50,000/MW financial security

requirement would result in approximately $57.5 million in posted security, less than one-third of

the project’s total cost. 31

        AEP’s Panhandle Transmission Project, submitted in February 2026, is estimated at nearly

$10 billion and is associated with 25 GW of project large load growth. Under the $50,000/MW

security framework, the corresponding large loads would collectively provide approximately

load growth carries a total transmission cost of $477 million, while a $50,000/MW requirement

would yield about $257 million in security, or just over half the project cost. 33

         While residential and small commercial customers may receive some incidental benefit

from upgraded transmission infrastructure, allocating the remaining costs to those customers risks

departing from cost causation principles and the intent behind SB 6. In these cases, the scale of

large load driven transmission expansion can result in system-wide upgrades that substantially

exceed what would otherwise be necessary to serve organic, population-driven growth alone,

creating a mismatch between cost responsibility and cost causation.

        This discrepancy is likely to intensify under the Batch Zero process, where dozens or even

hundreds of large load interconnection requests could collectively drive hundreds of billions of

dollars in additional RPG transmission investment. As the volume and concentration of large load

requests increase, so does the risk that residents will be footing the bill for speculative projects, as

well as projects that do ultimately materialize. If significant transmission assets are constructed in

reliance on projected large loads that do not fully materialize, existing customers may be left to

recover stranded or underutilized infrastructure costs.

        Without stronger alignment between financial responsibility and demonstrated load

certainty, there is a heightened risk that system-wide transmission expansion will be

disproportionately recovered from residential and small commercial ratepayers. This dynamic

underscores the importance of ensuring that financial security requirements and cost allocation

frameworks are sufficiently robust to reflect actual system drivers, particularly in a high-growth

environment where large load interconnections are becoming the primary driver of transmission

planning outcomes. OPUC recommends the Commission revert to its original proposed amount

for financial security based on a dollar per megawatt amount in the sum of $100,000 per MW. 34

        i.         Alternatively, phase the financial security amount based on the estimated
                  interconnection and transmission costs and require increased proof of the
                  customer’s financial capability.

       OPUC recognizes that several large load customers are on the smaller scale and may not

have the same financial capability as the bigger large load customers. OPUC supports business

development as this means increased jobs and economic growth for its customer classes.

Therefore, the agency is open to a phased financial security on a dollar per megawatt basis if doing

so would not jeopardize the large load customer from paying its interconnection and share of

system upgrade costs. As a trade-off for a lower financial security amount, the large load customer

must provide more stringent proof that it has the financial capability to contribute to the recovery

of all transmission and interconnection costs accrued to connect that customer to the grid.

Otherwise, without greater proof, the large load customer may end up not being able to pay for the

transmission costs, and those costs will ultimately be passed on to individuals, families, small

businesses, and other ratepayers.


       D. Define direct interconnection costs in CIAC broadly to include all facilities and
          equipment at and adjacent to the point of interconnection necessary to interconnect the
          large load customer.

       The PFP defines CIAC to include all of a large load customer’s “direct interconnection

costs,” which encompasses “all costs associated with facilities built to interconnect the large load

customer to the existing ERCOT system, including radial lines and substation upgrades necessary

to interconnect the new large load customer.” 35 OPUC is concerned that this may lead to a narrow

meaning of what must be included in CIAC. Therefore, OPUC recommends broadening the

definition to include “all costs associated with facilities and equipment built at and adjacent to the

 point of interconnection necessary to interconnect the large load customer to the ERCOT system.”

OPUC would then recommend broadening the enumerated list to account for facilities or

equipment that may be needed that are not specifically identified in the list in proposed

subparagraph (f)(9) by stating the following: “including but not limited to new or upgraded radial

lines and substations necessary to interconnect the large load customer.”

       OPUC recommends removing the word “new” from “large load customers” to include

those large load customers encompassed in the applicability provision in proposed

subparagraphs (b)(2) and (3). 36 OPUC also encourages the Commission to keep CIAC

non-refundable and allow for a true-up at the next comprehensive base rate or transmission cost of

service (TCOS) proceeding, whichever is applicable.

          E. Clearly define system upgrade costs and the process for determining the large load
            customers’ portion of such costs.

   recovery subject to true-up in future base rate or TCOS proceedings.
6. Clearly Define System Upgrade Costs: OPUC supports requiring large load customers
   to provide financial security for system upgrades but urges the Commission to adopt a
   broad, clearly defined scope of "system upgrades" and a transparent cost allocation
   methodology to avoid litigation risk and cost shifting, and to ensure any refunds or
   adjustments are deferred until final costs are determined in a base rate or TCOS proceeding.
7. Separate Rate Treatment and Minimum Demand Charges: OPUC supports
   incorporating minimum demand charges for large load customers (including a 10-15 year
   term) into the rule and recommends additional safeguards, such as cost recovery if
   operations cease early, alignment with transmission asset life and depreciation, limits
   preventing utilities from undercutting Commission-set requirements, and caution against
   assuming sustained high load growth when structuring the charge, to ensure durable and
   equitable cost responsibility.
8. Flexible Language for all Batch Study Processes: The rule should be drafted flexibly to
   ensure large load customers are responsible for all transmission costs necessary for
   interconnection, regardless of ERCOT review tier or process, and to accommodate
   potential changes, including the batch study process supplanting or modifying the current
   regional planning group framework.
Capacity Reallocation: Establish clear rules for the reallocation of large load customers'
outstanding financial commitments under PLJRA § 37.0561, including successor-in-interest
obligations and batch study participation, to ensure that any transferred, sold, or assigned large
load proj ect retains its financial responsibilities and that no interconnection-related costs are
shifted to other ratepayers due to gaps in assignment or enforcement.
Refundability: Limit refundability to dollar per MW financial security consistent with
PURA § 37.0561(i). Subject the other nonrefundable financial commitment options to a
Commission-approved true-up in a base rate or TCOS proceeding, where large load customer
receives bill credit or surcharge after comparing actual to estimated costs. This ensures that
any adjustments to CIAC, system upgrade costs, or other financial security are made only after
a final cost determination to prevent cost shifts to other ratepayers.
